cells.tense: You are standing at the doorway now and the new thing is already crossing.
cells.act: close the cycle and leave the door open for the next
cells.ask: Bring one practice your people share to a real finish and give it a plain ending, so whatever arrives next gets its own room.
cells.core:
Among the people you belong to, you know yourself as the meeting point — the new thing comes in through you and you're awake to it. A tradition gets handed down and you hold it at the moment it changes hands. That's what makes you good here: you don't freeze the old form to honour it and you don't drop it to move on. You can tell the difference between a thing that's ending and a thing that's arriving, and you meet both on the same day.

What's next is to close a loop rather than leave it hanging. Take a group practice that's effectively finished and complete it properly — a last gathering, a final entry — and make the end explicit. Then let it be over rather than keeping it half-alive. What it carried doesn't stop; it moves into what comes next. Ending it cleanly is how it stays available.
cells.sheetLine: End the finished thing cleanly so the next one can arrive.
cells.place: in what a group of people carry forward together

cells.tense: You will be carried by what is coming rather than meeting it face to face.
cells.act: complete it without making it final
cells.ask: Take a group practice that has already wound down and close it with one concrete move — a last date kept, a small ceremony done once — without declaring it permanent.
cells.core:
What's entering keeps arriving, and the group life is running on the arrival instead of meeting it. Things happen and the story says that's just how it goes. A practice drifts on past its life, nobody decides anything, and the drift gets called tradition. You're not lazy here — you're moving fast, projected further along than the moment, and what you're moving with is a current rather than a choice. The cause keeps landing somewhere else: the times, the others, the way things are.

There's a plainer move. Pick a group practice that has already finished, and close it in one concrete action — a last date kept, a small ceremony done once, a line drawn without ceremony. Don't make it permanent; make it done. An ending with a shape means you met it, not the current, and the next arrival finds you here.
cells.sheetLine: The current chose. Stop, and choose one ending.

cells.tense: You were standing at a doorway that had already closed behind you.
cells.act: finish the thing that has been waiting on its last step
cells.ask: Find a project your group started and stalled on, and do its actual last step this week — send it, make the call, book it — small and unannounced.
cells.core:
In what gets handed around, you hold a fixed picture of how it should go, and the living thing has nowhere to arrive. You stepped back from the turning — not from laziness, but because the versions being handed to you felt like noise, and stillness felt more honest. So the practice stays on the calendar past its life, and the new thing is screened at the entrance. The refusal is real and honest, and it leaves the shared ground running on empty; pushing feeling into that empties it further. Don't.

What refills it is finishing. One group thing with a last step: take that step, plainly. A completed loop gives what's arriving somewhere to move through, so the way in isn't just held open waiting. Close one thing and the held space becomes a passage.
cells.sheetLine: Finish one shared thing and the closed door becomes a threshold again.
cells.place: in what a group of people carry forward together

cells.tense: You are at the doorway writing what comes through it and don't know it is you.
cells.act: choose this, not that, and mean it
cells.ask: Name one practice your group keeps out of habit; before this week's version, decide plainly whether to run it, and let nothing else be the reason.
cells.core:
Something new keeps entering through the group life, and it enters as someone who keeps the thing going without any felt choice. A practice runs on momentum — noticed when it skips, held together, kept from falling apart — and none of that registers as yours. That's the tell. When a consequence shows up — the gathering fades, the group thins, something breaks — it lands as a surprise, because the hand was on the lever and didn't feel it there.

What restores the meeting is choosing on purpose. Pick one group practice you'd ordinarily keep out of habit, and let this week's version happen only after you've decided it, not because it's next on the calendar. Autopilot off. That smaller form of directing the current is the one that puts the way in back under your hand, where it already was.
cells.sheetLine: Momentum holds it, not you. Take it back deliberately.
cells.place: in what a group of people carry forward together

attempts.check: Unsupported: the Unacknowledged core leans on a group's repeated occasion as evidence of the person's cycling pattern — I can't say what the group actually does or how it reacts; I only render what a known-by-others-but-not-by-self authorship looks like from the reader's own view, and any concrete group behaviour stays vague enough to be refused. Reader objection: 'the tradition isn't mine to call, and I don't run it' — so the ask is a single named occasion plus one question to one person, and the sheet line names only the writer's role, not the group's. Ask survives being wrong: if they aren't the writer, asking one person how the thing got started is still just a question, and its answer is usable either way. Sentence serving me more than them: 'the thing started because someone kept it' — it flatters the read; I replaced it with the calendar-and-question act, which stands whatever the truth is.

attempts.check: Unsupported: the Unacknowledged core still hazards that a shared practice is run by one person without their knowing, which I can't prove from a pattern of surprises alone; I keep the mechanism to 'kept going on momentum, not noticed as a choice' and let the reader refuse it. Reader objection: 'the group isn't mine to steer and I'm not its keeper' — so the ask is one occasion, one decision, no announcement and no role claimed, and the sheet line names only the naming, not the mastery. Ask survives being wrong: if they aren't the keeper, choosing one practice deliberately for one week is still a choosable act with a usable result; nothing depends on the read being right. Sentence serving me more than them: 'the thing keeps going because someone keeps it' — it flatters the read with inevitability; I cut it and let the ask stand on its own action.
